claims.claim: Tennessee v. Garner, 471 U.S. 1, was decided March 27, 1985; White, J., wrote for six Justices and O'Connor, J., dissented joined by Burger, C.J., and Rehnquist, J.

Garner held that deadly force may not be used to prevent escape unless it is necessary to prevent the escape and the officer has probable cause to believe the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious physical injury to the officer or others, with some warning where feasible.

Garner held that using deadly force to prevent the escape of all felony suspects, whatever the circumstances, is constitutionally unreasonable, but did not hold the Tennessee statute unconstitutional on its face.

Graham v. Connor, 490 U.S. 386, decided May 15, 1989, held that all excessive-force claims arising from an arrest, investigatory stop, or other seizure of a free citizen are analyzed under the Fourth Amendment's objective reasonableness standard rather than substantive due process, displacing the Johnson v. Glick test.

Graham identified three non-exhaustive factors - the severity of the crime at issue, whether the suspect poses an immediate threat to the safety of officers or others, and whether the suspect is actively resisting arrest or attempting to evade arrest by flight.

Graham directs that reasonableness be judged from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene rather than with the 20/20 vision of hindsight, with allowance for split-second judgments in tense, uncertain, and rapidly evolving circumstances, and without regard to the officer's underlying intent or motivation.
42 U.S.C. Sec. 1983 creates a civil cause of action against a person who, under color of state law, deprives another of rights secured by the Constitution and federal law.

Harlow v. Fitzgerald (1982) shields government officials performing discretionary functions from civil damages liability insofar as their conduct does not violate clearly established statutory or constitutional rights of which a reasonable person would have known; Pearson v. Callahan (2009), a unanimous opinion by Alito, J., held that the two-step sequence is no longer mandatory in all cases.
18 U.S.C. Sec. 242 makes it a federal crime to willfully deprive a person of federally secured rights under color of law, with penalties escalating where bodily injury or death results.

34 U.S.C. Sec. 12601, enacted in 1994 and formerly codified at 42 U.S.C. Sec. 14141, authorizes the Attorney General to bring a civil action for equitable and declaratory relief to eliminate a pattern or practice of law enforcement conduct that deprives persons of federal rights; DOJ states that harm to a single person or an isolated action is usually insufficient and that the Section has no authority over federal law enforcement agencies.

The Justice Manual's use-of-force policy requires more than the constitutional minimum - deadly force only when necessary, no deadly force solely to prevent escape, prohibition of chokeholds and carotid restraints unless the deadly-force standard is met, de-escalation where objectively feasible, and duties to intervene and render medical aid - and states expressly that it creates no right or benefit enforceable at law or equity.

State criminal standards vary and can be stricter than the federal constitutional minimum; California permits deadly force only when the officer reasonably believes, on the totality of the circumstances, that it is necessary to defend against an imminent threat of death or serious bodily injury or to apprehend a fleeing person for a felony that threatened or resulted in death or serious bodily injury.

The FBI's National Use-of-Force Data Collection is voluntary; as of the FBI's May 8, 2025 Federal Register notice, 12,861 agencies were enrolled as possible respondents and the collection covers incidents resulting in death or serious bodily injury and firearm discharges at or in the direction of a person.

OMB set publication thresholds for the FBI collection in September 2018 keyed to the share of sworn officers represented (below 40 percent nothing publishable; 40-59 percent limited information; 60-79 percent most frequently reported responses; 80 percent or more unconditional), and GAO reported in December 2021 that participation as of November 2021 was 44 percent for 2019 and 55 percent for 2020.

In 2022 about 19 percent of U.S. residents age 16 or older (49.2 million) had contact with police, and 748,800 residents (1.5 percent of those with contact) experienced the threat or use of nonfatal force, compared with 1,045,600 (1.9 percent) in 2020, as measured by the BJS Police-Public Contact Survey and published in October 2024.

A 2021 Lancet study comparing the National Vital Statistics System with three open-source databases estimated 30,800 deaths from police violence in the USA between 1980 and 2018 (95 percent uncertainty interval 30,300-31,300) and estimated that 55.5 percent of those deaths were unreported in the NVSS.
In June 2018 there were 17,541 state and local agencies performing law enforcement functions in the United States, each of which sets its own use-of-force policy.

A 2020 systematic review found 64 de-escalation training evaluations over 40 years, mostly outside policing, with few adverse consequences and slight-to-moderate improvements but questionable evaluation quality; a 2022 stepped-wedge randomized controlled trial in the Louisville Metro Police Department reported reductions of 28.1 percent in use-of-force incidents, 26.3 percent in citizen injuries, and 36.0 percent in officer injuries after ICAT training.

NIJ's CrimeSolutions rates body-worn cameras Ineffective for their effects on officer use of force (profile posted January 2022, drawing on a 26-study meta-analysis by Lum and colleagues, 2020) and rates crisis intervention teams Ineffective for reducing trained officers' use of force in encounters involving people with mental illness (profile posted October 2018, five studies analyzed by Taheri, 2016); both profiles carry a notice that they are no longer updated.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether de-escalation training reduces police use of force
positions: Engel, McManus and Herold (2020) concluded from a systematic review of 64 evaluations that the evidence base was of questionable quality and that no study had shown de-escalation training reduces force in the field.

Engel, Corsaro, Isaza and McManus (2022) reported statistically significant reductions in use-of-force incidents and injuries after ICAT training in a stepped-wedge randomized controlled trial in one large agency.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports both, in order, and states that the 2022 trial is one agency, one curriculum, and one period - encouraging evidence rather than a settled finding. It does not generalize the Louisville percentages to other agencies.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many people are subjected to police force in the United States each year
positions: The FBI's agency-reported collection is voluntary and has not met its publication thresholds.
The BJS Police-Public Contact Survey produces national estimates from residents' reports but excludes fatal encounters.
Independent databases and the 2021 Lancet modeling estimate substantially more fatal cases than official vital statistics record.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents no single number as the national count. It names each source, states what that source measures and cannot measure, dates each figure, and labels the Lancet figures as modeled estimates with an uncertainty interval.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether body-worn cameras reduce use of force
positions: Cameras are widely adopted on the theory that observation changes behaviour.
CrimeSolutions rates the practice Ineffective for effects on officer use of force based on a 26-study meta-analysis.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the CrimeSolutions rating and its date and notes that the profile is no longer updated, rather than asserting a permanent conclusion.

sourceRecords.title: Tennessee v. Garner, 471 U.S. 1 (1985)
sourceRecords.provider: Supreme Court of the United States (U.S. Reports, digitized by the Library of Congress)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the full official U.S. Reports opinion PDF (fetched with curl and a browser user-agent; the WebFetch tool received HTTP 403 from tile.loc.gov). Supports: argued October 30, 1984 and decided March 27, 1985; White, J., for the Court, joined by Brennan, Marshall, Blackmun, Powell, and Stevens, with O'Connor, J., dissenting joined by Burger, C.J., and Rehnquist, J.; apprehension by deadly force is a seizure subject to the Fourth Amendment's reasonableness requirement; the use of deadly force to prevent the escape of all felony suspects, whatever the circumstances, is constitutionally unreasonable; deadly force 'may not be used unless it is necessary to prevent the escape and the officer has probable cause to believe that the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious physical injury to the officer or others'; where feasible, some warning should be given; and the Tennessee statute was unconstitutional as applied to an apparently unarmed, nondangerous fleeing suspect but not unconstitutional on its face. Short quotations from a U.S. government work. URL aligned to the govinfo U.S. Reports scan already in the registry; the Library of Congress scan of the same opinion is what this worker read.

sourceRecords.title: Graham v. Connor, 490 U.S. 386 (1989)
sourceRecords.provider: Supreme Court of the United States (U.S. Reports, digitized by the Library of Congress)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the full official U.S. Reports opinion PDF (curl with a browser user-agent). Supports: argued February 21, 1989 and decided May 15, 1989; Rehnquist, C.J., for the Court, with Blackmun, J., concurring in part and in the judgment joined by Brennan and Marshall, JJ.; the holding that all claims of excessive force - deadly or not - in the course of an arrest, investigatory stop, or other seizure of a free citizen are analyzed under the Fourth Amendment's objective reasonableness standard rather than substantive due process; rejection of the Johnson v. Glick four-factor 'maliciously and sadistically' test; the three named factors ('the severity of the crime at issue, whether the suspect poses an immediate threat to the safety of the officers or others, and whether he is actively resisting arrest or attempting to evade arrest by flight') introduced by the non-exhaustive word 'including'; 'judged from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene, rather than with the 20/20 vision of hindsight'; the split-second-judgments passage; the statement that the inquiry is objective 'without regard to their underlying intent or motivation' and that evil intentions do not make a violation out of objectively reasonable force; and the point that the Eighth Amendment standard applies only after the State has secured a formal adjudication of guilt.

sourceRecords.title: Harlow v. Fitzgerald, 457 U.S. 800 (1982)
sourceRecords.provider: Supreme Court of the United States (U.S. Reports, digitized by the Library of Congress)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the official U.S. Reports PDF. Supports the qualified immunity formulation used in the lesson: government officials performing discretionary functions generally are shielded from liability for civil damages insofar as their conduct does not violate 'clearly established' statutory or constitutional rights of which a reasonable person would have known, and the Court's replacement of the earlier subjective good-faith element. Powell, J., delivered the opinion of the Court.

sourceRecords.title: Pearson v. Callahan, 555 U.S. 223 (2009)
sourceRecords.provider: Supreme Court of the United States (U.S. Reports, digitized by the Library of Congress)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the official U.S. Reports PDF. Supports: argued October 14, 2008 and decided January 21, 2009; Alito, J., delivered the opinion for a unanimous Court; the two-question qualified immunity framework (whether the facts alleged or shown make out a violation of a constitutional right, and whether that right was 'clearly established' at the time of the alleged misconduct); and the holding that the Saucier v. Katz sequence should no longer be regarded as mandatory in all cases, leaving lower courts discretion over which question to address first.

sourceRecords.title: 18 U.S.C. Sec. 242 - Deprivation of rights under color of law
sourceRecords.provider: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (mirror of the U.S. Code)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the statutory text. Supports the federal criminal standard used in the lesson's compare/contrast: liability attaches to whoever, under color of law, 'willfully' subjects a person to the deprivation of federally secured rights, with penalties escalating where bodily injury results, where a dangerous weapon is used, and where death results.

sourceRecords.title: Justice Manual 1-16.000 - Department of Justice Policy on Use of Force
sourceRecords.notes: Read the full policy page (curl with a browser user-agent). Supports the lesson's example of agency policy sitting above the constitutional floor: DOJ officers may use deadly force only when necessary, meaning a reasonable belief that the subject poses an imminent danger of death or serious physical injury; deadly force may not be used solely to prevent the escape of a fleeing suspect; chokeholds and carotid restraints are prohibited unless the standard of necessity for deadly force is satisfied (subsection updated January 2025); officers are trained in de-escalation, which should be employed if objectively feasible; affirmative duties to intervene and to request or render medical aid (sections updated July 2022); and the express statement in 1-16.700 that the policy 'is not intended to, and does not, create any right or benefit, substantive or procedural, enforceable at law or equity.' The lesson names the restraint categories the policy names and does not describe any technique.

sourceRecords.title: Conduct of Law Enforcement Agencies (Special Litigation Section)
sourceRecords.provider: Civil Rights Division, U.S. Department of Justice
sourceRecords.notes: Read the page (curl with a browser user-agent); page footer states 'Updated February 25, 2025.' Supports: the Special Litigation Section enforces the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act provision now codified at 34 U.S.C. Sec. 12601; it may act on a pattern or practice that systemically violates rights, and harm to a single person or an isolated action is usually not enough; it has no authority to investigate federal law enforcement agencies and cannot assist in individual criminal cases; and its settlements and court orders frequently require improved investigation and review of uses of force, training and supervision, data collection, and independent oversight.

sourceRecords.title: Does de-escalation training work? A systematic review and call for evidence in police use-of-force reform
sourceRecords.provider: Engel, R. S., McManus, H. D., & Herold, T. D., Criminology & Public Policy 19(3), 721-759 (2020)
sourceRecords.notes: Bibliographic record and publisher-deposited structured abstract retrieved from the Crossref API (the Wiley full text is not openly accessible). Supports: the systematic review identified 64 de-escalation training evaluations across a 40-year period, primarily in nursing and psychiatry; outcomes showed few adverse consequences and slight-to-moderate individual and organizational improvements; and the authors' conclusion that findings are limited by the questionable quality of almost all evaluation designs, leaving the effect of de-escalation training on police behavior unsettled. Only the abstract was read; no article prose was reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Assessing the impact of de-escalation training on police behavior: Reducing police use of force in the Louisville, KY Metro Police Department
sourceRecords.provider: Engel, R. S., Corsaro, N., Isaza, G. T., & McManus, H. D., Criminology & Public Policy 21(2), 199-233 (2022)
sourceRecords.notes: Bibliographic record and publisher-deposited structured abstract retrieved from the Crossref API. Supports: a stepped-wedge randomized controlled trial evaluating the Police Executive Research Forum's ICAT de-escalation training in the Louisville Metro Police Department beginning in 2019; reported statistically significant post-training reductions of 28.1 percent in use-of-force incidents, 26.3 percent in citizen injuries, and 36.0 percent in officer injuries; and the authors' own statement that before this study no research had empirically demonstrated that de-escalation trainings reduce use of force in the field. Only the abstract was read.

sourceRecords.title: Fatal police violence by race and state in the USA, 1980-2019: a network meta-regression
sourceRecords.provider: GBD 2019 Police Violence US Subnational Collaborators, The Lancet 398(10307), 1239-1255 (2021)
sourceRecords.notes: Full abstract retrieved through the NCBI E-utilities PubMed API (PMID 34600625); the PubMed record states the article is open access under CC BY 4.0. Supports: the study compared the National Vital Statistics System with three non-governmental open-source databases (Fatal Encounters, Mapping Police Violence, and The Counted) and used network meta-regression to estimate under-reporting; it estimated 30,800 deaths (95% uncertainty interval 30,300-31,300) from police violence in the USA between 1980 and 2018, and that the NVSS did not report 55.5 percent of them; and it reported the highest age-standardised mortality rate in non-Hispanic Black people. The lesson presents these as the authors' modeled estimates with uncertainty intervals, attributes the authors' interpretive framing to them, and does not present any figure as a national count.

sourceRecords.title: California Penal Code Sec. 835a - Use of force by peace officers
sourceRecords.notes: Read the current section text, which the page states was amended by Stats. 2025, ch. 241, sec. 24 (SB 857), effective January 1, 2026. Used as one worked example of how a state criminal-law standard differs from the federal constitutional minimum: deadly force is justified only when the officer reasonably believes, based on the totality of the circumstances, that it is necessary to defend against an imminent threat of death or serious bodily injury or to apprehend a fleeing person for a felony that threatened or resulted in death or serious bodily injury where the officer reasonably believes the person will cause death or serious bodily injury unless immediately apprehended; the requirement, where feasible, of identification and a warning before deadly force; and the statutory definitions of deadly force, imminent, and totality of the circumstances. The lesson states that this is California law only and that state law varies.
